analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination based on sex, sexual orientation, and gender identity in stores, services, and transportation.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 82 Democratic cosponsors and zero Republican cosponsors, was referred to a House Judiciary subcommittee in September 2017, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Civil Rights Act of 1964 to make it illegal for businesses open to the public — stores, salons, banks, shelters, online retailers, taxis, airlines, and service providers — to refuse or segregate customers because of their sex, sexual orientation, or gender identity. It would also confirm access to restrooms and locker rooms consistent with a person's gender identity, extend protection to people associated with or perceived as members of a protected group, and bar businesses from using a religious-liberty defense to escape these rules. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBT people, women (including pregnant women), and people associated with or perceived to be members of those groups. Today, federal law bans discrimination in public accommodations based on race, color, religion, and national origin — but not sex, sexual orientation, or gender identity, so a customer can be refused service in many states with no federal recourse. The bill would close that gap in everyday transactions: shopping, banking, travel, shelter, health care, and legal or accounting services [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: LGBT people and women facing discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Adds sex, sexual orientation, and gender identity to the Civil Rights Act's ban on discrimination and segregation in public accommodations, giving LGBT customers and women a federal cause of action when they are refused service.

Covers places and services the 1964 law predates: online retailers and service providers, salons, banks, gas stations, food banks, shelters, travel agencies, funeral homes, health care providers, and transportation services like taxis, buses, and airlines.

Explicitly protects restroom, locker room, and dressing room access consistent with a person's gender identity, and protects people who are associated with, or merely perceived to be, members of a protected group — even if the perception is wrong.

Defines sex to include sex stereotypes and pregnancy, childbirth, and related medical conditions, so a business could not treat a pregnant customer worse than a customer with any other physical condition.

Bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 from being used as a claim or defense against these protections, closing what supporters saw as a loophole that would let businesses refuse service on religious grounds.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses open to the public would bear the cost of compliance: retailers, salons, banks, online sellers, transportation providers, shelters, funeral homes, and health care, accounting, and legal service providers would face new federal nondiscrimination obligations and possible lawsuits. The burden falls hardest on small operators and on owners with sincere religious objections to serving, for example, same-sex couples, since the bill would expressly remove the RFRA defense. The bill creates no public subsidy; the cost is legal exposure and changed business practices [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Retailers, service providers, and religious-objector businesses

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is religious liberty: by overriding RFRA as a defense, the bill would leave wedding vendors, religious shelters, and other faith-based providers no exemption from serving customers whose relationships or identities conflict with their beliefs — courts could not even weigh the claim.

The bill defines 'establishment' to cover anyone whose operations affect commerce and says an establishment need not be a physical place, sweeping in solo professionals and online sellers and creating litigation risk for small businesses over where the line falls.

Opponents also objected to the shared-facility provision: the bill would make it unlawful to deny restroom, locker room, or dressing room access consistent with gender identity, a rule critics said raises privacy concerns in intimate settings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people the bill covers, the benefit is concrete: a federal right to buy a cake, rent a car, book a flight, get a bank account, or enter a shelter without being turned away because of who they are — a right that federal law simply does not provide today. The costs are real but narrower: compliance burden on small businesses and the removal of any religious-liberty exemption, which is the honest trade-off at the heart of the dispute. An honest supporter would acknowledge the RFRA override is absolute; an honest opponent would acknowledge the status quo leaves LGBT customers and pregnant women with no federal remedy in much of the country.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its civil rights subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the Customer Non-Discrimination Act on July 27, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On September 6, 2017, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice — the last action of any kind recorded for it.
Eighty-two House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; the cosponsor list shows no Republicans.
The bill stayed parked in committee until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and every bill not passed by then dies and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that opposed the new obligations — particularly those with religious objections to serving LGBT customers — are better off, because the federal nondiscrimination rules never took effect. Status quo discrimination remains lawful in states without their own public-accommodation protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Businesses that avoided the new rules

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 44 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 44 original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Bob Goodlatte

sides.party_line_note: All 82 cosponsors were House Democrats and none were Republicans; the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without any vote being recorded.

industries.industry: Retail, hospitality, and consumer service businesses
industries.note: Stores, shopping centers, salons, gas stations, and funeral homes would become covered public accommodations and lose the ability to turn away LGBT customers or pregnant women. The public gains a federal right to service; the businesses gain legal obligations and exposure to discrimination suits.

Taxis, car services, trains, buses, airlines, and travel agencies would be newly covered, so a driver or airline could not refuse or segregate passengers based on sex, sexual orientation, or gender identity.

industries.industry: Online retailers and platform service providers
industries.note: The bill would extend public-accommodation law to online retailers and service providers for the first time, a notable expansion since the 1964 law predates e-commerce and has generally been read as covering physical places.

Providers with sincere religious objections — wedding vendors, religious shelters, faith-affiliated service centers — would have their strongest legal shield removed, because the bill bars RFRA from being raised as a claim or defense against these rules.
Independent doctors, accountants, and lawyers serving the public would be covered even without a storefront, since an establishment need not be a physical facility.
